title: AI in LA Courts: David Slayton on Access to Justice — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: David Slayton

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source focuses on risk-tiered AI assistance for self-represented litigants and preserving human escalation in access-to-justice settings. It does not address whether automating junior lawyers’ work threatens apprenticeship, verification expertise or the future training pipeline.
qs: I see AI as a tool, not a replacement—it’s a tool.
Think about it from the perspective of a self-represented litigant, and maybe even from a triage perspective.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: Slayton accepts the cluster’s case for bounded AI augmentation and adds a concrete court-administration response: using AI to process rising document and case volumes amid chronic staffing shortages. He also links faster processing to possible litigant cost reductions, while treating both AI-driven filing growth and downstream benefits as hypotheses or expectations rather than measured outcomes. He does not address the cluster’s central concerns about direct-user verification, unequal risk or remedies.
qs: It’s like: either we choose to use AI to help us process all these documents that are coming in and deal with the cases, or we say we're going to keep doing it our old-fashioned way because we're not embracing AI—and we'll just get run over.
Well, AI helps us with some of that—certainly with the too slow piece, because we can use it to help expedite some things, therefore maybe reducing the cost.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source accepts that AI adoption alone cannot close the justice gap and materially develops a risk-aware delivery model: informational triage for self-represented litigants, low-risk testing with user feedback, escalation to further help, and concentration of lawyer attention on high-stakes matters. It also reinforces the cluster’s evidentiary caution because these are practical proposals rather than measured access-to-justice outcomes.
qs: I see AI as a tool, not a replacement—it’s a tool.

So I'm curious about your thoughts on thinking through different ways to select uses that are low-risk—identifying those and rolling out opportunities to test and get feedback from self-represented litigants there—versus the more high-stakes situations where we would want to focus lawyer time and attention (and the promise of AI) to help move lawyers more in that direction.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, human-led deployment and materially extends the cluster with a court-specific operating model: bounded official-source tools for initial guidance, escalation to human services, user-feedback loops, and problem-led risk management centred on access and public trust.
qs: I see AI as a tool, not a replacement—it’s a tool.

I think making sure that we are purposefully pursuing AI in ways that help us solve problems (again, not just pursuing AI for its own sake, but to solve problems), while also keeping in mind the risks that come with it and the things we need to do to protect against those issues—that’s the balance.

st.t: Civil justice: Capacity gains need human safeguards
st.an: The source directly supports using AI to expand meaningful access while keeping assistance tiered and risk-sensitive rather than replacing lawyers. Its Court Help example illustrates bounded self-help, and it reserves lawyer attention for higher-stakes matters while acknowledging implementation risks and institutional barriers.
qs: I see AI as a tool, not a replacement—it’s a tool.

So I'm curious about your thoughts on thinking through different ways to select uses that are low-risk—identifying those and rolling out opportunities to test and get feedback from self-represented litigants there—versus the more high-stakes situations where we would want to focus lawyer time and attention (and the promise of AI) to help move lawyers more in that direction.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: Slayton directly supports evaluating court AI against the harms, access gaps and capacity limits of the existing system rather than an idealised human alternative. He advocates problem-led, bounded adoption that preserves human assistance and weighs potential access and processing gains against bias, delegated judgment and loss of public trust.
qs: A system without AI—a system without new technology—has failures and risks as well, and they are significant.

I think making sure that we are purposefully pursuing AI in ways that help us solve problems (again, not just pursuing AI for its own sake, but to solve problems), while also keeping in mind the risks that come with it and the things we need to do to protect against those issues—that’s the balance.

st.t: Justice capacity: AI potential requires deliberate implementation
st.an: Slayton supports the proposition that technology can reduce barriers to civil justice when paired with deliberate process improvement. He defines success as informed, empowered access rather than guaranteed case outcomes, while offering aspirations and near-term expectations rather than measured access gains.
qs: We're beginning to use technology to say it doesn't matter whether you have a lawyer or not, whether you have money or not, whether you can get to court or not, or whether you have prior knowledge—we're going to give you tools that allow you to access the justice system in ways.
So as we think about embracing these things and re-looking at our processes to make things work better, to me that's the most exciting thing that keeps me going every day.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: Slayton’s firsthand use of a public-facing court navigation tool and ChatGPT supports the cluster’s emphasis on practical, everyday experimentation before technological certainty. His account is narrow and anecdotal: it indicates perceived convenience and faster access to court information, but does not demonstrate reliability, access-to-justice outcomes or a broader redesign model.
qs: And then the other thing I'll say, professionally, is we launched a new website at the court—LACourt.gov—on July 1st, and we have a generative AI tool right on the home screen to help people.

It's called “Court Help,” and I'm now using that to find anything on our website, because rather than clicking around and trying to find it, it's just so much faster to say, “Hey, take me to the strategic plan,” and it takes me right to it.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: Slayton supports active engagement with technology rather than waiting for certainty, especially by combining adoption with court-process review. He reinforces the cluster’s public-interest framing: technology should reduce barriers and enable informed participation, without promising successful outcomes or presenting measured proof of effectiveness.
qs: You may lose even with all that information, we're not saying we want to make people win or lose; we want to give them information.
So as we think about embracing these things and re-looking at our processes to make things work better, to me that's the most exciting thing that keeps me going every day.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s framing of legal AI as organisational and service redesign rather than a software purchase. It links adoption to court-service goals, identifies cultural and change-management barriers, and advocates leadership-enabled frontline experimentation, practical workflows and continued human assistance. Its access-to-justice claims remain prospective rather than quantified outcomes.
qs: In addition to the barriers that are cultural, legal, and regulatory to transformation, there's just a big change-management hill to climb in providing court services to a largely unrepresented user base.

The message is: this is a tool that can really help employees with the work they're already doing, and we want them to be demanding it from us (versus us trying to push it down on them and them resisting it).

kp.k: Large court workloads coincide with severe representation gaps
kp.d: Slayton describes L.A. Superior Court as having 582 judges and commissioners, 36 courthouses across over 4,700 square miles, about 5,000 employees, a $1.1 billion budget, and about 1.3 million annual case filings. He reports that 70%–80% of family litigants, depending on the year, start or finish without representation. Work with Stanford on eviction cases found only 14% of defendants represented in the last year, compared with what he recalls as 94% of landlords; he says the gap grew over the several years examined. These figures establish the access and capacity problems motivating AI adoption, rather than demonstrating AI's effects.
qs: there are about 1.3 million cases filed per year in the court across our litigation types.
In our family context, depending on the year, somewhere between 70% and 80% of the people navigating the family system either start off or end up the case representing themselves.

only 14% of defendants in the last year in our eviction cases were represented by a lawyer. That’s compared to, I think, 94% of landlords being represented by a lawyer—only 14% of tenants had a lawyer.

kp.k: Court strategy prioritizes effectiveness and user access
kp.d: Discussing the 2025–2028 strategic plan identified by Leonard, Slayton describes a 6- or 8-month planning process involving 21 judges. The court deliberately replaced efficiency with effectiveness in its mission and adopted an accessibility, trust, and justice vision. He frames AI as one possible means of transforming the user experience, with court users' needs taking priority alongside staff and judicial officers, rather than speed or technology adoption as ends in themselves.
qs: It's now that we will be effective.
let's not just do things to do it fast; let's do it well.
Our court will be accessible to all, trusted by all, and just for all.
We want to use data to inform our decisions.

kp.k: Court Help provides navigation and procedural guidance
kp.d: Slayton reports that LACourt.gov launched on July 1st with a generative AI tool, Court Help, on its home screen. He uses it to locate website material and describes its ability to supply step-by-step eviction-response instructions and links to forms. Its content is based on the court's website and the Judicial Council of California's website. This is a reported deployment for public information access, not a reported replacement for legal representation.
qs: we launched a new website at the court—LACourt.gov—on July 1st, and we have a generative AI tool right on the home screen to help people.
So you can go on Court Help right now and say, “How do I file a response or an answer to an eviction case?” and it gives you step-by-step instructions and links to the forms.

kp.k: AI safeguards combine controlled sources, disclaimers, and feedback
kp.d: Slayton says Court Help was trained to use only court and Judicial Council content, with further tuning of its creativity. He recommends scrutinizing source information for bias, acknowledges possible errors through a disclaimer, and describes thumbs-up/thumbs-down feedback informing improvements. He argues risks should be compared with existing system failures and imperfect human assistance, not a risk-free baseline; no measured accuracy or bias results are provided.
qs: One is we trained that tool to only use content from our website or from the Judicial Council of California.
And then we're fine-tuning that tool to tell it how creative to be.
we put a disclaimer on there: “This might not be right.”
then we take that information as a feedback loop and we try to make improvements to the system.
A system without AI—a system without new technology—has failures and risks as well, and they are significant.

kp.k: AI should triage needs rather than replace people
kp.d: Slayton endorses Leonard's distinction between lower-risk information assistance and higher-stakes situations needing lawyers. He proposes an initial AI information layer sufficient for an unspecified share of users, followed by referral to self-help staff when needs exceed the tool's capabilities. Under limited funding and staffing, he sees AI as extending service capacity while preserving human guidance, rather than substituting robots for lawyers.
qs: I see AI as a tool, not a replacement—it’s a tool.
Maybe level one is an AI tool that helps provide them information to move them along the path.
Okay, now you need to go to the self-help center, or you need to call the self-help center, because this tool is not going to help you beyond this point.
I think of AI as a tool that's sort of a force multiplier.

kp.k: User research reveals persistent demand for human reassurance
kp.d: Slayton recounts a Stanford Law School project investigating why people visited self-help centers despite online alternatives. Focus groups and other research, reported back a couple months later, challenged his initial hypothesis that users should shift remotely: people feared mistakes in exceptionally important life events and wanted personal confirmation. He uses this finding to qualify technological substitution and support retaining people for needs beyond information provision; no sample size is stated.
qs: They did focus groups and all this research, and they came back to me a couple months later
Because this is the most important thing happening in their lives, and they're terrified they'll get it wrong.
So sometimes that human touch is so important, especially in situations where people have so much at risk.
But we've got to have the people there to assist when those needs rise above what we can provide through technology.

kp.k: Administrative innovation requires pilots and tolerance for failure
kp.d: Slayton recommends clearly diagnosing problems and explaining why change is needed, conducting small pilots, learning quickly from failures, and making decisions despite incomplete information. He distinguishes the need to avoid mistakes in case decisions from an administrative culture whose intolerance of error can prevent experimentation. Successful changes, or effective recovery from failures, build trust for larger initiatives.
qs: Change for change’s sake is not going to be successful.

Obviously, when we're deciding cases we don't want to be making mistakes (there is an appellate process for that, if we do), but I think that sometimes spills over into our administrative functions: “Let's not make any mistakes.”
We want to manage failure, but we are going to fail.
Give it a shot on a smaller scale and see if it works—see what doesn't work—and figure out how to make it happen.
Then when you're successful—or you fail, but you're able to pivot and make it successful—then you get some trust.

kp.k: Staff literacy should drive bottom-up AI adoption
kp.d: Drawing an analogy from a Harvard Business Review account of Moody's, Slayton says the court is on the cusp of providing basic AI understanding and safe tools so employees identify and request applications themselves. He contrasts this with top-down mandates likely to generate fear and resistance. In a predominantly union-represented workforce, his stated message is assistance with existing work rather than job elimination. He also asserts that judges and staff already use AI, whether leadership knows or not.
qs: It's coming to us, and our staff and our judges are using it whether we know it or not.
Let's give them actual tools that they can use safely and effectively in their everyday functions.

The message is: this is a tool that can really help employees with the work they're already doing, and we want them to be demanding it from us (versus us trying to push it down on them and them resisting it).
something I could take and do in my own organization, and we're on the cusp of doing that.

kp.k: AI-driven filing growth remains a hypothesis
kp.d: Slayton reports substantial increases in unlimited civil filings, defined as cases exceeding $35,000 in controversy, mostly involving personal injury auto, some debt, and lemon law cases. He attributes to a recent National Center for State Courts discussion, using L.A. and a couple other states' data, the hypothesis that AI-developed pleadings contribute to growth. He argues that without additional resources courts need AI-assisted processing to cope; the transcript provides neither growth rates nor a causal finding linking AI to filings.
qs: we are seeing tremendous increases in unlimited civil case filings (civil case filings where the amount in controversy is over $35,000), mostly driven by personal injury auto cases, some debt cases, and lemon law cases.

There's a hypothesis (the National Center for State Courts wrote on this recently, using our data and a couple other states’ data that look very similar to ours) that AI-developed pleadings are driving some of this.
Quite frankly, we're not getting additional resources to deal with those.

kp.k: Document automation reallocates staff attention to complex work
kp.d: Slayton reports that the court is beginning to use AI and robotic processing for 20 relatively straightforward document types representing 1 million annual filings. He says this relieves staff's processing queues and allows more attention to documents demanding greater judgment. The volume describes the selected document types, not a stated audited count of completed AI processing, and no quantified time savings are supplied.
qs: But now we're beginning, even in our court, to use AI and robotics processing to process documents.
Those 20 document types represent 1 million documents filed per year.

It's tremendously helpful to make our staff not feel so overwhelmed with the queues of documents coming in and allows them to spend more time on the ones that take more of their brainpower to process.

kp.k: Both slow and reckless adoption threaten public trust
kp.d: Slayton predicts that failing to adopt AI risks overwhelmed courts, continuing delays and costs, and declining public confidence. Conversely, adoption that creates bias or the perception that AI rather than judges decides cases could erode trust even faster. He advocates purposeful, problem-specific implementation with safeguards; his anticipated improvements in speed and potentially cost are not presented as measured outcomes.
qs: Well, AI helps us with some of that—certainly with the too slow piece, because we can use it to help expedite some things, therefore maybe reducing the cost.

if it gets to a point where people say, “Oh, the judges aren't really making decisions—they're using AI,” or we're using AI in ways that introduce bias that causes people to lose trust, those are huge risks.
If we move too fast, we ultimately lose trust probably faster than by doing nothing.

kp.k: Optional predictive resolution pathways are a future possibility
kp.d: Responding to McCormack's question about future human versus AI interaction, Slayton speculates that court case data could support predictive analytics describing typical outcomes and an optional faster resolution pathway. He conditions this possibility on user acceptance and effective tools, while preserving access to a full conventional process. He analogizes to online dispute resolution and the choice between remote and in-person appearances; he does not report an implemented AI adjudication system.
qs: I think we could use AI and the data set of cases we have to provide some predictive analytics to people, to let them know what a typical outcome would look like.
Maybe people would choose to take that path—sort of like an express lane path.
always having the option, I think, to go through the full major “five lanes of traffic” model.
I would really love to give people choices similar to that when it comes to adjudication of their cases.

kp.k: Access ambitions concern participation, not guaranteed favorable outcomes
kp.d: Slayton sees appropriately deployed AI, alongside process redesign and remote technology, as an opportunity over the next couple of years to expand meaningful access regardless of representation, money, travel ability, or prior knowledge. His stated aim is to inform and empower participation rather than ensure users win. This is an aspiration for improved access, not evidence that equal access has already been achieved.
qs: in the right situations and employing those tools appropriately, to use AI to drastically expand people's ability to access justice in really meaningful ways.
You may lose even with all that information, we're not saying we want to make people win or lose; we want to give them information.
I think the opportunities ahead of us in the next couple of years are tremendous.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: David Slayton describes existing AI-assisted court navigation and document processing, and predicts expanded access, greater court capacity and potentially optional AI-assisted resolution pathways.
pts.d: Slayton makes the following distinct claims. (1) Court Help makes court information easier and faster to find and supplies step-by-step procedural instructions and form links, including for answering eviction cases. (2) AI can act as a triage tool and a force multiplier for scarce self-help and legal resources: some users may obtain sufficient information from the tool, while others should be directed to human assistance. He explicitly presents this as assistance rather than replacement. (3) The court is beginning to use AI together with robotic processing for 20 routine document types representing one million annual filings; he says this relieves staff queues and frees attention for more demanding documents. (4) He reports a hypothesis that AI-developed pleadings contribute to rising civil filings by making it easier for lawyers to file documents. He argues that courts need their own AI capabilities to cope without additional resources. (5) AI can expedite court work and might consequently reduce litigant costs; failure to adopt it could undermine public confidence as courts struggle to serve users. (6) Conversely, overly rapid or biased deployment, or a perception that AI rather than judges makes decisions, could erode trust even faster than inaction. (7) As a future possibility, AI applied to the court's case data could show typical outcomes and support an optional faster resolution pathway, while retaining a full conventional process. He does not announce an implemented AI adjudication system. (8) Providing staff with AI understanding and safe tools could generate employee-led demand for useful applications rather than resistance to management-imposed adoption. His broader prediction is that appropriately deployed AI can substantially expand meaningful access to justice.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists mainly of Slayton's operational experience, deployment examples, court workload and representation figures, reported Stanford research, and a reported NCSC hypothesis; the episode supplies no quantified AI accuracy or impact evaluation.
pts.d: For Court Help, Slayton cites a live deployment and his own experience using it to find material faster than navigating the website. For document processing, he gives the number of selected document types and their annual filing volume, alongside a qualitative account of staff benefits; he does not quantify processing-time savings, error rates or completed automated transactions. For the access problem, he reports that 70–80% of family-system users begin or end their cases self-represented and that work with Stanford found only 14% of eviction defendants represented in the preceding year, compared with approximately 94% of landlords. These figures describe existing need, not measured AI effects. Stanford Law School focus groups and related research reportedly found that users attended self-help centers because the stakes and fear of mistakes made human reassurance important. That supports his qualification that online availability does not eliminate demand for people. For AI-induced filing growth, he cites recent National Center for State Courts writing drawing on L.A. and other states' data, explicitly labeling the explanation a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated causal finding. He identifies personal injury auto, debt and lemon law cases as contributors to growth in unlimited civil filings. His adoption approach draws on his court-administration experience and an HBR account of Moody's as an analogy, not an evaluated L.A. AI training program. Predictions about cost reductions, trust, expanded access and optional AI-assisted resolution are reasoned expectations; no direct outcome study or benchmark is provided for them.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Slayton distinguishes tools already launched or beginning deployment in 2025 from near-term organizational plans and undated, conditional possibilities for AI-assisted adjudication.
pts.d: Court Help was launched with the new court website on July 1 in the context of this 2025 episode. AI and robotic document processing are described as beginning at the court, not as a completed court-wide transformation. Staff education and bottom-up adoption are plans the court is on the cusp of implementing. The conversation situates innovation within the 2025–2028 strategic plan, while Slayton anticipates substantial opportunities over the next couple of years. He gives no implementation date for predictive analytics or an express resolution pathway. Those possibilities depend on public comfort, effective tools and user choice, with the conventional process remaining available. He qualifies the access claim by acknowledging that the fraction of users sufficiently helped by AI alone is unknown and might be small; human staff must remain available when needs exceed technological assistance. Risk mitigation for Court Help includes limiting source content to court and California Judicial Council websites, adjusting creativity, warning that answers may be wrong and using thumbs-up/thumbs-down feedback to improve responses. He advocates purposeful problem-solving, smaller pilots and learning from limited failures, not adopting AI for its own sake. Faster processing is a claimed opportunity; reduced costs are explicitly tentative. His risk comparison includes harms of the existing non-AI system rather than assuming the status quo is risk-free.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal beneficiaries envisaged are unrepresented court users and resource-constrained court staff; lawyers, judges and the wider public are also affected through filing practices, service delivery and institutional trust.
pts.d: Self-represented litigants, particularly family litigants and eviction defendants, could gain usable procedural information, forms and referrals without first navigating complex websites or traveling to a self-help center. Slayton also frames the opportunity around users facing financial, geographic, technological, language and knowledge barriers, without claiming that AI has already removed each barrier. Users facing high-stakes matters may still need human reassurance and guidance. Self-help staff and lawyers could concentrate scarce resources on people needing more intensive assistance. Court processing staff could shift attention from routine documents to work requiring greater judgment; Slayton's stated framing is augmentation, not an announced reduction in jobs, and he specifically recognizes union concerns. Attorneys may increasingly interact with automated back-end processing without knowing it and may use AI to generate filings more readily. Judges and administrators face the combined pressures of growing workloads, limited resources and responsibility for trustworthy deployment. Parties might eventually choose between faster AI-assisted resolution and conventional proceedings. The public is affected through both the possibility of better access and the risk of diminished confidence in judicial decision-making. Slayton explicitly separates access and empowerment from guaranteeing favorable case outcomes.
